305.history: The harbour on the headland was settled from Cnoc ghorm, and in the fourth century its households lived under Lagh an Loscaidh Bhig like every other. In FE 398 the household of Murchadh Ruadh lost its right for a third offence and went down to the strand to fish rather than beg cold porridge from its kin. On a calm morning some years after, Cailean Buidhe's boat was lost in water that lifted under it, and two of the five came home. A year to the day later the strand set out a bowl for the five and spoke the boat's name once over it. The wake was kept after that. Anndra Cìobair, who had swum home, poured its first cup for near forty years. The coast's households took turns carrying driftwood to the relit beacon on the headland. In the twenty-eighth century two more of its boats felt the sea breathe under them, and one did not come home.
305.known_for: the wake for the lost boat, and the thing under it

119.history: Fishers of the east founded the harbour. In the last century of the age its people gave boats and men to the watch against the island raiders, and Sliochd Raghnaill gave the town a place on the council at Dùn ìseal beside its own seat. Tormod Donn, the uncle who claimed An Talla Dearg against Mòr nic Coinnich, kept his house here and withdrew his claim from here by his steward's word. He died at Cuan ruadh eleven years later, and his line ended with him.
119.known_for: its boats for the watch, and Tormod Donn's house

462.history: The blind Keeper Fionnlagh Dall was laid in FE 184 in the ancient unclaimed burying-ground near Cnoc dhìreach, the first burial there any living hand had set down by name. Coimheadaichean na Lasrach hallowed the ground that season, and it has been Tuam Cnoc dhìreach since. Calum Beag, who walked the whole eleven days at the head of the litter, carried a plain stone there on his own back in his old age and set it at the grave-head. In the last years of the age the town on the carriers' road south of the springs became known for a heavy undyed cloth that the carriers wore on the high passes.
462.known_for: the blind Keeper's burying-ground, and the carriers' cloth

502.history: Herders of the eastern plain founded the hill town, and at the end of the age its dyers learned to fix a pale blue from a hill plant that grew nowhere lower. The carriers' cloth of the whole mountain country was dyed here. Only Coimheadaichean na Lasrach kept theirs undyed, holding that a flame kept for no one's blood needed no colour to show whose it was.

202.history: The millers of the deep race founded the town in the eastern hills, and at the end of the age a water-mill was built here to grind the grain of the mountain districts' common granaries. The miller took one measure in sixteen and no more, and the provincial roll calls it fair, a word it uses of few millers.

256.history: Drovers of the south-east founded the town at the ford. In FE 2,875 rain on the eastern hills brought the river over the ford and carried off the carriers' shelter and six of the townsfolk. The district's common granary stood on a rise the flood never reached, and it fed the town through the winter that followed. The roll sets the drowning and the granary down side by side and says nothing more.
256.known_for: the flood and the granary on the rise

110.history: The old harbour of the Seann-Dhaoine on the south-eastern coast took, at the end of the age, to laying oyster-beds in the shallows below the town. Its people held that the craft had come with the name of their town. The clerks of the provincial roll set the claim down and marked it doubtful.

326.history: Households of the south coast founded the town, and at the end of the age a mill and a shrine came to share one roof here. The miller kept the shrine's handful of grain beside his millstones as faithfully as he kept his sixteenth measure. Coimheadaiche na Lasrach's cutter who came to try it found the handful kept and the flour good, and wrote that and no more.

37.history: The old harbour of the Seann-Dhaoine on the northern coast became, in the last century of the age, the home of the whole northern fishing fleet. Its boatbuilders shaped the longest craft the island knew, built for a single day's run along the coast and never meant for open water.
37.known_for: the long boats of the northern fleet

92.history: Sailors of the south-west founded the harbour on the western coast. At the end of the age the families of its drowned took up the custom of holding a feast on the shore each year with an empty place set for each of the lost, and the custom spread up the coast as far as Seann Warr.

433.history: Households of Imrich nam Pantar founded the town in the south-west. At the end of the age potters of Baile ghorm set up new kilns here, where the clay ran better and the wood was nearer, and the hard red ware of the western road was made here for the rest of the age.

318.history: Households who came for the spring of the holy hill founded the town. They kept a shrine to the ancestors and to the sìth of their own hill in the old folk way, with no hawk in it, no wolf, no sting and no stag. Clàr an Talla of rites set them among the keepers of Na Seann Spioradan, a company by then as settled and separate as any of the eight.
318.known_for: the ancestor-shrine of An Seann Urram

311.history: The valley-folk of the eastern narrows founded the town. When drought emptied the granary of Achadh shean at the end of the age, grain went from Baile chaol under Lagh a' Bhìdh Roinnte, and its rolls set down the repayment measure by measure to the last. The clerk added that no such debt in the roll had ever before been repaid in full.

411.history: Farming households founded the town in the east. In FE 2,900 a dry summer burned its pastures and left the common granary empty by spring. Grain came up from Baile chaol and Cuan ruadh under Lagh a' Bhìdh Roinnte of Lachlann Bàn and Raonaid Dhubh, and the district repaid it harvest by harvest.
411.known_for: the drought and the repaid grain

9.history: Inis mhin, a small fishing harbour on the northern shore, came into the rolls only once in An Aois Naomh, when its headman walked the whole way to the wool-fair at Inis mhòr to lay a complaint against the road-guard's toll. The complaint is kept in full, a longer telling than the harbour otherwise earned. A clerk of Inis mhòr wrote in the margin that a small harbour's whole history on the page might be the one grievance it once walked far enough to voice.
